prize_parts.citation: for formalising and empirically testing how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic development

statement.case_for: Persson and Tabellini built political economics into a systematic field. It has explicit models of how electoral rules and forms of government shape taxation, spending and public goods, and these generate testable predictions that were then confronted with cross-country and within-country data. Besley adds state capacity, accountability and political selection, which links the programme to development and public economics. The work is about three decades old, widely replicated, extended and taught, so the Committee can judge its durability with confidence. After hearing colleagues, I still regard it as a coherent, mature, attributable contribution with broad influence on public economics, development and comparative politics. B005 is also an excellent candidate, and I rate it highly on the common criteria of breadth of use, clean attribution to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, and maturity. I keep B014 first because it explains policy choices and institutional design, which I weigh as at least as important as a methods toolkit. That is my own judgement, not something support counts can settle.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is identification. Much of the evidence on constitutional and electoral-rule effects is cross-country and observational, and it is less clean than the design-based work I would normally weight most heavily. A second concern is the overlap with the 2024 institutions prize, which makes it harder to argue that this is a distinct contribution rather than a neighbouring one. A third is that others (Alesina, Drazen and Acemoglu-Robinson-type work) contributed nearby, so any three-name credit set leaves some disputes open.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B014 second. He argues that it formalises how constitutions and electoral rules shape policy and covers different ground from the 2024 institutions prize. He also concedes that causal identification of constitutional effects is harder than in natural-experiment settings and that the Committee may be wary of recognising institutions again soon.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction. The 2024 prize concerned long-run institutions and prosperity, while this programme concerns how specific political rules map into fiscal and policy choices. I also agree that the identification limits are real, and I would not defend the cross-country estimates as design-based. My case rests on the theory-plus-evidence programme and the agenda it set, not on any single clean causal estimate. A citation should be worded to avoid overclaiming causal findings.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B005 first. He argues that BLP demand estimation and dynamic industry models changed IO and are used in merger review, trade, health and environmental analysis. He regards the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes attribution as clean, with Bresnahan the main alternative. He ranks B014 third as high-impact and mature but possibly too close to the 2024 prize.
responses.response: I accept that B005 has the cleaner attribution and very broad use, and I ranked it third myself. Where I differ is on weighing. A methods prize is only as valuable as the questions it lets us answer, and structural results are sensitive to functional-form and equilibrium assumptions. I would not treat the number of colleagues who ranked it first as evidence of merit. I name B005 as my main alternative and would support it over weaker options if the Committee does not converge on B014.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B014 first. He sees a unified framework from theory to systematic empirics that opened a field now standard across economics and political science. He regards the three-person credit set as coherent and the timing as ripe, while flagging overlap with the 2024 prize.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the coherence of the trio. I am more cautious than he is about the overlap. It is the most likely objection from other members, and I think the citation must explicitly separate policy outcomes under political rules from the long-run institutions agenda. I also agree that adding other political economists would dilute a credit set that is already at the three-person limit.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B014 seventh. She credits it as a unified body of work with testable implications. She worries that the historical-political strand overlaps with Acemoglu-Robinson, that novelty may be reduced after 2024, and that the empirical identification of constitutional effects is imperfect.
responses.response: I take the identification and overlap points seriously, and they are my own main reservations. I would qualify the overlap point. Persson and Tabellini's core is formal political-economic theory applied to fiscal and policy outcomes, whereas the 2024 work is mainly about colonial and historical origins of institutions. I concede that Besley's state-capacity strand sits closer to that agenda and is the part of the credit set most exposed to the objection. If the Committee insists on that distinction, a Persson-Tabellini core is the fallback.

uncertainties: Whether a majority will treat B014 as distinct from the 2024 institutions prize or as too close to it.
How much weight the weaker, mostly cross-country identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects should carry against design-based candidates.
Whether Besley's state-capacity strand belongs in the same award as the Persson-Tabellini constitutional programme, or whether a two-person Persson-Tabellini award would be cleaner.
Whether B005's broad methodological reach should outweigh B014's substantive questions, and whether Bresnahan or Levinsohn is the better third name there.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile that requires recusal. I overlapped institutionally at Stockholm University (2010–17) with the IIES macro group, but the profile records no co-authorship with any credited name on B014, B005 or B025. I make no claim about connections beyond the profile.
